options: It makes model binding faster
It replaces the need to define request DTOs
It centralises validation, so `if (!ModelState.IsValid)` isn't repeated, or forgotten, in every endpoint
It validates the JWT before the controller runs
questions.explanation: Without a filter the same check is repeated in every endpoint, is easy to forget and clutters controllers. The filter sets `context.Result` to a `BadRequestObjectResult` when the model state is invalid.

questions.prompt: Why does a `ValidationFilter` that only checks `context.ModelState.IsValid` still report FluentValidation rule failures?
options: FluentValidation automatically adds its errors into `ModelState`
The filter calls each validator's `Validate` method itself
FluentValidation throws an exception that the filter catches
FluentValidation rewrites the action's return value
questions.explanation: With `AddFluentValidationAutoValidation()`, rule failures such as "Title is required" end up in `ModelState`, which is exactly what the filter inspects.

source.section: How to use Validation Filter (clean approach) with fluent validation

questions.prompt: What is the main risk of applying the filter with `[ServiceFilter(typeof(ValidationFilter))]` instead of `options.Filters.Add<ValidationFilter>()`?
options: The filter runs twice on every request
If you forget the attribute on a new endpoint, that endpoint has no validation
It can't be combined with `[ApiController]`
It applies to every controller, so you can't exclude a health check
questions.explanation: `[ServiceFilter]` gives granular control but is high maintenance. The global registration is "set it and forget it", at the cost of making exclusions harder.

questions.prompt: Whichever way you apply it, what does the lesson say you must do first?
options: Remove `[ApiController]` from every controller
Mark the filter class `static`
Call `app.UseMiddleware<ValidationFilter>()`
Register the filter in DI with `builder.Services.AddScoped<ValidationFilter>()`
questions.explanation: Both the global registration and `[ServiceFilter]` require `ValidationFilter` to be registered in the DI container first.

questions.prompt: Why does the project put registrations in `ServiceCollectionExtensions.AddApplicationServices()`?
options: To move DI code out of `Program.cs`, keeping startup clean and modular
Because services can't be registered directly in `Program.cs`
To make every service a singleton
To register validators automatically by scanning the assembly
questions.explanation: Without extensions `Program.cs` grows huge and hard to maintain. `builder.Services.AddApplicationServices()` groups the registrations, which keeps startup clean and makes them reusable.
